commons:60946201.summary: On this large silver chalice, a gilded arcade frames standing figures; here Christ, haloed and holding a book, raises his right hand in blessing beneath an arch, with a Greek inscription running around the rim above. The Met notes that the chalice carries images of Christ and the Virgin with saints and archangels, so that when it was raised at the Eucharist the congregation saw Christ's own image on the cup of his blood.
facts: Its Greek dedication asks prayers for the repose of the soul of Anastasia and the salvation of John, deacon of Saint Stephen of the village of Attarathion, according to the Met.
The cup holds about 1.5 litres, a generous size that, as the Met suggests, could be seen by a large congregation.
It is one of several chalices in the Attarouthi Treasure (Met 1986.3.5).
commons:60946201.notes: Met object ID 466139, accession 1986.3.5 (identified via the Commons file).

commons:60921233.summary: This view of the ivory bucket shows, in the upper register, the betrayal of Christ: Judas presses close to kiss the haloed Christ while soldiers seize his arm, one raising a club. In the lower register a seated, bearded figure rests his head on his hand as an angel approaches, beside other scenes continuing around the vessel. Carved in panels divided by bands set with gilt foil, the situla once held the holy water used to bless the faithful, uniting the liturgy with the story of salvation.
facts: The Met dates the situla to 860–880 and attributes it to northern France; its subjects, according to the museum's tags, include the Annunciation, the Baptism of Christ and the Last Supper, on faces not seen in this photograph.
It stands about 21 cm high with the handle raised and was given to The Met by J. Pierpont Morgan in 1917 (accession 17.190.45).
A situla is a bucket-shaped vessel; in the medieval Church such buckets held holy water for sprinkling during the liturgy.
commons:60921233.notes: This photograph (view s4) shows only some of the scenes. The lower-register scene with the seated figure and angel was not identified with certainty (possibly Joseph's dream).

cur:catacombs-mp-bust-of-christ.summary: A bearded Christ with long dark hair and a large nimbus looks out frontally, his right hand raised, the letters Alpha and Omega painted at either side. Unlike the youthful shepherd of earlier catacomb art, this is the majestic, bearded Christ of the late 4th century, proclaimed as the beginning and the end.
facts: Commons dates the painting to the late 4th or early 5th century.
The Alpha and Omega, from Revelation, became a common attribute of Christ in late 4th-century Roman art.
Painting reproduced from Joseph Wilpert, Die Malereien der Katakomben Roms (Freiburg, 1903), whose plates were photographed in the catacombs and hand-coloured in front of the originals.

cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.summary: Seated on a globe between angels and holding the scales of justice, the haloed Christ turns toward a crowd of the wicked at the left, while the righteous stand at the right beside a cross-staff. Above runs the verse 'thou satest in the throne judging right'.
facts: The manuscript came to Württemberg under Duke Charles Eugene (its sale is first mentioned in 1787) and has been in the library at Stuttgart since at least 1818.
The Stuttgart Psalter was made around 820–830 at the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés near Paris; its 168 leaves contain the psalms with 316 coloured miniatures set between the verses they illustrate.
cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.notes: Image from the WLB digital facsimile (Public Domain Mark), showing the whole page with the miniature.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-9-christ-.summary: At the top of a crowded two-part drawing the Christ-Logos sits in a globe-mandorla between angels with cross-staffs, holding a pair of scales as the judge of the nations. Below, the psalmist stands on a tower above 'the gates of death' while soldiers slay their victims, and the wicked lie in wait for the poor. The page illustrates the long Vulgate Psalm 9, which joins the Hebrew Psalms 9 and 10.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
Its text is written in rustic capitals, an archaic script that once led scholars to date the manuscript to the 6th century; the drawings are now recognised as Carolingian.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-9-christ-.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-88-christ.summary: In the middle of the top register the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos, holding an open scroll, sits in a globe-mandorla resting on personifications of the sun and moon and surrounded by groups of saints and angels, while personifications of Mercy and Truth approach the psalmist. The rest of the crowded drawing, with ships, cities and armies, illustrates the long psalm on God's covenant with David. It is one of the most densely populated pages of the manuscript.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
After centuries in England the manuscript arrived in Utrecht in 1716; it is often called the most valuable manuscript in the Netherlands.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-88-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:monumental-tokali-descent-from-cross.summary: The pale body of Christ is taken down from the cross: Joseph of Arimathea, at the left, embraces it as it is lowered, while Nicodemus, at the right, bends to draw the nails from the feet. The surface is worn and scratched with graffiti, but the tender handling of the dead Christ remains clear.
facts: Tokalı Kilise ('Church of the Buckle'), the largest church at Göreme, comprises an Old Church of the 10th century, painted in strips of red and green, and a larger New Church of the late 10th or early 11th century whose walls are dominated by rich indigo blue made from lapis lazuli.

cur:monumental-tokali-descent-from-cross.notes: The photograph shows a detail of the wall; whether the scene belongs to the Old or the New Church is not stated in the source. Dates for both phases are debated (c. 910s–920s for the Old Church; mid-10th to early 11th century for the New).

feat:sainte-chapelle-passion-window.summary: At the very center of the apse of King Louis IX's palace chapel, directly behind the raised tribune where the relics of the Passion, including the Crown of Thorns, were displayed, glows the window of Christ's Passion. Its medallions, in deep reds and blues, narrate the events of Holy Week, from the Last Supper and the betrayal through the scourging to the Crucifixion. The whole chapel was conceived as a jewel-like reliquary in glass, and this window placed the story of Christ's suffering immediately above the relic of that suffering.
facts: Louis IX built the Sainte-Chapelle to house the Crown of Thorns, bought from the Latin Emperor Baldwin II of Constantinople for 135,000 livres — more than three times the 40,000 livres the chapel cost to build and glaze.
The chapel's fifteen great 13th-century windows contain more than a thousand narrative scenes, and nearly two-thirds of the original medieval glass survives.

After the Revolution the upper chapel served as an archive (1803–1837) and some glass was removed or lost; the windows were restored in 1846–1855 and taken down for safekeeping during the Second World War.
The chapel was consecrated on 26 April 1248, remarkably soon after construction began around 1241–1244.
